subject: Critical Thinking
title: Medical Ethics: Triage and Impossible Choices
description: One-minute skill: Medical Ethics: Triage and Impossible Choices.

hook.text: COVID-19: one ventilator, two patients. One is 30, otherwise healthy. The other is 70 with heart disease.

buildup.text: Medical triage: allocating scarce resources when not everyone can be saved.

discovery.text: Common triage principles: save the most lives, save the most life-years, first-come first-served, random lottery, or.

twist.text: Each principle has moral trade-offs. 'Most life-years' discriminates against the elderly.

climax.text: Ethical frameworks guide triage, but they cannot erase the tragedy inside the choice.

punchline.text: The choice isn't between right & wrong. It's between wrong & worse.

quiz.question: Why is medical triage ethically difficult?
options: Every allocation principle has moral trade-offs; no principle avoids all unfairness

details.summary: Medical triage forces healthcare workers to decide who gets scarce resources when not everyone can be saved. These decisions crystalize abstract ethical theories into life-and-death practice under extreme time pressure.
details.whyItMatters: Pandemics, disasters, and resource shortages make triage ethics unavoidable for healthcare systems worldwide.
takeaways: Triage prioritizes patients based on urgency and survivability
Utilitarian, egalitarian, and lottery approaches all have trade-offs
Pre-established protocols reduce moral distress during crises

faq.question: What ethical frameworks guide medical triage decisions?
faq.answer: Utilitarian triage maximizes lives saved, egalitarian approaches treat all equally via lotteries, and some frameworks prioritize the worst-off or youngest patients.

faq.question: Why is pre-planning for triage ethically important?
faq.answer: Decisions made in crisis are prone to bias and emotional error. Pre-established, transparent protocols ensure fairness and reduce the psychological burden on individual clinicians.
